blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Distinguish the quantity of a factor of production from its quality, explain what causes the quantity and quality of labour, land, capital and enterprise to change, and analyse what a change in each does to output and to incomes.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: Counting units against weighing units
blocks.text: The quantity of a factor is how much of it is available: the number of workers, the hectares of land, the count of machines. The quality of a factor is how productive each unit is in use: the skill and health of a worker, the fertility of soil, the age and precision of a machine. Quantity counts units; quality measures what each unit yields. An economy can have many workers and low output per worker, or few workers and high output per worker - both patterns are found among real economies, and the difference between them is quality, not quantity.

blocks.heading: What changes the quantity and quality of labour
blocks.text:
The quantity of labour is the number of people available and willing to work. It changes with the size of the working-age population, which depends on past birth rates and death rates. It changes with net migration: workers arriving from abroad add to it and emigrants subtract from it. It changes with the ages at which people leave school and retire - raising a retirement age from 60 to 65 keeps older workers in the labour force for five more years. And it changes with the participation rate, the share of working-age people who work or seek work; more childcare places, for example, can let more parents take paid jobs.

The quality of labour is how productive each worker is. It rises with education and training, which add skills, and with better health care and nutrition, which mean fewer days lost to illness and more energy at work. It can fall when skilled workers emigrate: several southern African health services have lost trained nurses to richer countries, which cuts the quantity and the quality of their health workforce at once.

blocks.heading: What changes land, capital and enterprise
blocks.text:
Land. The quantity of usable land can rise when land is reclaimed - the Netherlands has drained large areas of sea and lake to create farmland - or when exploration finds new mineral or energy deposits. It falls when soil erodes, when overgrazing and drought turn grazing into bare sand, which is desertification, or when forests are cleared and the soil washes away. The quality of land rises with fertilisers, irrigation and drainage, which raise what each hectare yields, and falls with overuse and pollution.

Capital. The quantity of capital rises when firms and governments invest in new machines, buildings and infrastructure, and falls through depreciation as existing capital wears out or becomes outdated. In a year when investment is smaller than depreciation, the stock of capital shrinks. Its quality rises with technological progress: a new machine built with newer technology tends to produce more per hour than the one it replaces.

Enterprise. The number of people starting and running businesses tends to rise where registering a business is cheap and quick, where taxes on profit are lower, where small-business loans are available and where people are willing to take risks. It tends to fall where regulation is heavy or the economy is unstable, because the expected reward then seems too small for the risk. The quality of enterprise rises with education, business training and experience, which improve how well entrepreneurs organise the other factors and judge risk.

blocks.heading: The same forty machinists
blocks.text: Oshakati Textiles ran a two-year training programme for its machinists. Before the training, 40 machinists produced 1 200 shirts a week; after it, the same 40 machinists produced 1 600 shirts a week. The quantity of labour did not change: 40 machinists before, 40 machinists after. The quality rose. Output per machinist went from 1 200 divided by 40, which is 30 shirts a week, to 1 600 divided by 40, which is 40 shirts a week, a gain of 40 - 30 = 10 shirts per machinist each week. The firm now fills larger orders without hiring, and the trained machinists command higher wages, because a more productive worker is worth more to any employer who bids for them.

blocks.heading: Two routes to the same goal
blocks.text: The garment industry of Vietnam took the quantity route in its early years: farms released workers into city factories, and output rose mainly because more hands were at the machines. The planners then met the question such economies face - growth from adding hands slows once the flow from the farms thins, so training colleges followed the factories to raise the quality of the workers already there. Adding units and improving units are the two routes an economy has, and the second tends to matter more once the first has run its course.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Raising the quality of labour is the aim of the education and training spending that topic 4.3 follows through government budgets, and the extra output it releases is what shifts the production possibility curve of topic 1.4 outward.
